newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business press - Jan 5.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business press - Jan 5.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
SUNDAY TELEGRAPH
-- PERRY WILL CHAIR DEMERGED CENTRICA

Former chairman of Unilever, Michael Perry, is tipped to become chairman of Centrica, British Gas's retail and supply business, following its demerger. British Gas's chairman, Richard Giordano, has decided to forward his departure from Centrica to allow the group to develop an identity and to avoid a conflict of interest since he will remain chairman of BG, the production and pipeline business.
-- RYANAIR SETS COURSE FOR 100 MILLION STG LISTING

Irish entrepreneur, Tony Ryan, is considering an attempt to join the stock market through Ryanair, his airline founded in 1985. A market float should value the airline at more than 100 million stg. Ryan has stepped down as chairman in favour of David Bonderman, the former US civil rights lawyer whose Texas Pacific fund management group is regarded as the shrewdest in aviation.
-- BRANSON PLANS ONE BILLION STG ROLLING STOCK ORDER

Virgin Group is planning one of the largest orders in British history with a one billion stg order for new trains if it wins the bidding for the privatisation of the West Coast Main Line. If Virgin wins it will be expected to replace the existing rolling stock at a cost of 750 million stg, as well as its commitment to buy 250 million stg of rolling stock for its CrossCountry franchise.
-- FORMER MGM BOSS JUMPS US BAIL

Former Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer film mogul, Giancarlo Parretti, has skipped bail and fled the US, for his own town of Orvieto in Italy, days before being sentenced to a ten year prison sentence for perjury and tampering with evidence. US police have issued a warrant for Parretti's arrest.
SUNDAY TIMES
-- HOUSE PRICES 'TO RISE 50 PER CENT IN NEXT THREE YEARS'

Estate agents Savills have forecast a return to 1980s-style house inflation of 12 per cent this year and that values will rise over 50 per cent in the next three years. The production of annual double-digit growth is the highest forecast yet on house inflation and it is likely to fuel concern that the economy is overheating and may cause concern at the Bank of England.
-- BAE, ROLLS SEEK END TO FOREIGN LIMIT

Sir Ralph Robins, chairman of Rolls-Royce, and Sir Richard Evans, chief executive of British Aerospace, are urging the government to scrap the limit on foreign shareholdings imposed when the two groups were privatised in the 1980s. They believe the 29.5 per cent ceiling on overseas investment is outmoded, an obstacle to shareholder value and could restrict the companies' scope for strategic expansion.
-- WRAY AND SCHOLAR AIM TO BUY FOREST

One of Britain's top property investors, Nigel Wray, is poised to make a bid for Nottingham Forest football club before a shareholder meeting tomorrow. Wray is working with former Tottenham Hotspur chairman Irving Scholar and together they will offer Forest investors an alternative to the 13 million stg bid from a consortium led by Sandy Anderson.
-- ROVER LOSES 100 MILLION STG DESPITE SOARING SALES

According to Germany's Manager Magazine, Rover cut its losses by almost a fifth last year but still recorded a deficit of more than 100 million stg. Rover is expected to announce its sales exceeded 500,000 in 1996, the highest level for eight years, and that for the first time in its history it sold more vehicles overseas than in Britain.
THE OBSERVER
-- GRANADA HOTELS SALE RUNS INTO TROUBLE

Granada, the leisure and media group, is set to miss its self-imposed deadline of the end of January for selling its 17 Exclusive hotels. This has led to City warnings that the company's share price will slide if buyers are not found within the next few weeks. The group has sold just three of its properties and is having problems selling the 320 million stg Grosvenor House hotel.
-- TESCO TRIUMPHANT IN THE BATTLE OF THE CHRISTMAS GROCERIES

According to new figures from market research company AGB, which monitors buying by thousands of households, Tesco, the supermarket group, achieved its highest-ever share of the groceries market in the run-up to Christmas, continuing to increase its lead over Sainsbury, Asda and Safeway. None of the food retailers have yet given information about its performance over the Christmas period.
-- NEW CAR SALES REACH TWO MILLION

New car sales in the UK have broken the two million barrier for the first time since 1990. Consumer confidence has been rising steadily in the last eight months. Despite the recovery, there are still questions over the strength of the top three car manufacturers in the UK, Ford, Rover and Vauxhall, which continue to lose market share.
-- NEW CODE OF CONDUCT AIMS TO THUMP GAZUMPERS

There is to be an extension of the ombudsman scheme for housebuyers and sellers dissatisfied with the work of large estate agency chains to include the entire industry in July. Organisers backing the complaints system launched a code of conduct that includes rules against gazumping. Agents must now obtain specific instructions from sellers if a property is to stay on the market after an offer has been accepted.
-- STORM OVER HONDA'S PLANS FOR CAR DEPOT IN RURAL WILTSHIRE

Honda, the Japanese car giant, is facing protests from environmental groups and local government over its application to build one of the biggest car depots in the country outside the market town of Warminister in Wiltshire. Honda plans to use the site as a storage depot to serve its 180 UK dealers.
-- HOSPITALS FACE MORE GAS CUTS

The unprecedented demand bought by the cold weather has forced TransCo, the distribution arm of British Gas, to shut off supplies to all customers south of Birmingham with "interruptible" contracts. This will mean that some of Britain's largest NHS hospitals will face another week of gas cuts. British Gas predicted a "record number" of interruptions this winter and reminded consumers on such contracts, which are 25 per cent cheaper than those that guarantee supply, that it could interrupt supplies for up to 45 days.
-- CRACKDOWN ON LEAKS BY PR FIRMS

The DTI, the Stock Exchange and a number of practitioners are to press for a crack down on insider dealing and leaks of price sensitive information in financial public relations firms. They are to press for progress on a voluntary code of conduct of the industry after initiatives begun last year stalled.
-- BA MAY GIVE WAY TO SECURE US DEAL

New conditions are being discussed between British Airways and the Office of Fair Trading for clearance of BA's proposed alliance with American Airlines. If BA were prepared to make further concessions on take-off and landing slots at Heathrow, it could head off opposition to the deal from US carriers and pave the way for the alliance to be sealed in the next few months.
-- TEMPO LOOKS AT FLOAT TO FINANCE STORES

Britain's fifth largest electrical retailer, Tempo, is looking at a stock market flotation to help fund an expansion programme throughout the country, by opening another 11 large stores in 1997. Turnover is set to pass the 100 million stg mark this year. Growth this year is set to push Tempo into fourth position in the sector, ahead of Tandy and behind Powerhouse.
-- GERMAN PROPERTY FUNDS TARGET BRITAIN

The latest targets of cash-rich German property funds DEGI, DESPA and CGI, the most active players last year in the UK commercial property market, are regional shopping centres and office developments. German property funds accounted for nearly one billion stg of purchases in 1995 and 1996, including the Lloyd's building in London and St Enoch shopping centre in Glasgow.
MAIL ON SUNDAY
-- ALARM OVER POUND'S THREAT TO ECONOMY

According to Roger Bootle, chief economist at investment bank HSBC and one of the 'six wise people' who advise Chancellor Kenneth Clarke, there will be two interest rate raises before June, a booming pound and devastation for British industry. He fears that further strengthening of the pound will cause considerable damage by pricing exporters out of foreign markets.
-- CHILLING COST OF THE BIG FREEZE

The cold weather in Britain will adversely affect the construction, transport and manufacturing industries. The Association of British Insurers estimates that insurance companies will be faced with a barrage of claims. It is also bad news for the retail sector as shoppers opt to stay indoors.
-- BAR WARS BLOWS FUSE IN AT NUMBER TWO

Cadbury is set to publish its chocolate market review with the news that its Fuse chocolate bar has become the second most popular chocolate bar, outselling Mars by 25 per cent. Cadbury's says the bar spearheaded is 1996 drive for new products and is now second to Kit-Kat, which has been the most popular bar for ten years.
-- TAX REP STINGS LABOUR

A warning, in a booklet from Hargreaves Lansdown, a top financial adviser and issuer of direct mail, to investors about life under a Blair administration has been criticised by Labour's Treasury spokesman, Mike O'Brian, as 'misleading, mischievous and slapdash claptrap'.
-- RAILWAY DEAL RUNS LATE AT FIDELITY

Fidelity Brokerage, the American-owned share dealing giant, is asking 300 clients to pay for Railtrack shares, seven months after they bought them. The Securities and Futures Authority is to inspect Fidelity before a self-imposed ban on new business is lifted. BMC +44-171-377-1742
